text.p: French car parts supplier Valeo will regroup its industrial operations in Europe into larger plants centred on specific activities, chairman Noel Goutard said on Tuesday.

He said the regrouping would not necessarily translate into closures or layoffs. "The regrouping of several small plants into one agglomeration on a larger site isn't a drastic move," he told reporters after a news conference on the 1996 results.
By concentrating certain activities in certain sites, "you'd get the effect of rationalisation without plant closures," he said. Valeo has 62 plants in Europe, 27 of them in France.
"There may be some moves from one plant to another, but we have work for all," Goutard told the news conference.
Finance Director Thierry Morin told reporters the budget set aside for restructuring in 1997 was between 300 and 350 million francs, roughly even with 1996 levels.
Goutard said he expected the number of employees this year to remain roughly unchanged from last year's level of 32,500. Half of them were employed in France.

Valeo's productivity gains per person rose by 5.8 percent in 1996, but Goutard said that increase was insufficient given the price and cost pressures on suppliers. "At constant staff levels, I'd like productivity gains of at least 10 percent a year," he said.

Goutard said he expected 1997 sales to exceed 30 billion francs, compared with 28.87 billion for 1996, and he said he was confident the group would reach its objective of 40 billion francs in sales by the year 2000.

He made no profit forecast, but said he was encouraged by the economic climate in Europe characterised by low interest rates, weak inflation and more favourable foreign exchange parities resulting mainly from the rise the dollar and sterling.
Goutard said Valeo would revert in 1997 to its traditional dividend payout ratio of between 30 and 35 percent.
The ratio was 70 percent for 1996 due to an extraordinary dividend paid in November related to the sale of Cerus's 27.4 percent stake in Valeo to CGIP, its biggest shareholder.

Goutard said Valeo's relations with all its shareholders were "excellent." He said the group had no plans to raise capital in the markets but added that "if an opportunity presented itself...we could take advantage."
